title: Don't Look Up
synopsis: You found the comet. You also have to do a morning show. The comet does not care about ratings. Neither, soon, will you.

nodes.text: Your grad student runs it a fourth time because the third time was insulting. Six miles wide, 188 days, and a margin of error you could park a Subaru in. Nobody screams. Somebody's playlist is still going in the next room, an upbeat thing about summer. You listen to the whole song before anyone speaks.

choices.text: Call NASA before anyone else
choices.consequence: You dial the planetary defense office and get a phone tree. Option four is 'other.' You press four and describe the end of the world to a beep.

choices.text: Call your sister, just to say it out loud
choices.consequence: Your sister is at a soccer game. You say the number out loud to her and it becomes real in a way the spreadsheet never managed. You call your sister, just to say it out loud. It gets you to Morning TV, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Three days later, a beige room in Washington. The Chief of Staff eats a protein bar in six bites and asks what the ask is. You say the ask is the planet. He writes PLANET? on a legal pad. The President's daughter leans in to ask whether the lighting in here reads green.

choices.text: Demand a direct meeting with the President
choices.consequence: You raise your voice by maybe fifteen percent. Everyone in the room adjusts their posture, as though you'd done something to the carpet. You choose to demand a direct meeting with the President. By The Tech Billionaire, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Brief the science adviser thoroughly first
choices.consequence: You do it properly: forty slides, peer review, an appendix. He thanks you warmly and forwards the whole thing to a man named Dustin. You choose to brief the science adviser thoroughly first. By The Viral Clip, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: University PR has booked you on a show that just ran a segment on breakfast smoothies. The host says keep it fun. You brought three slides. He puts two of them up upside down and says, delighted, 'Look at that little guy go.' The little guy is the comet. The audience goes aww.

choices.text: Be respectful and try to be heard
choices.consequence: You stay pleasant, hit your talking points, and get eleven seconds before a weather hit. Pleasant, you learn, is a kind of mute button. You commit to be respectful and try to be heard. The road to The Tech Billionaire is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Lose your composure on air
choices.consequence: You say the word 'dying' four times in nine seconds. The host laughs, because on this show everything is a bit, including that. You choose to lose your composure on air. By The Viral Clip, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Peter's company makes a phone that claims to sense sadness. His plan: break the comet into commercially useful pieces, retrieve the rare metals, save the world and the quarter. He speaks slowly, like a hostage negotiator or a wind chime. When you ask for the engineering review, he says the review made him feel unheard.

choices.text: Refuse and demand a public mission
choices.consequence: You say no in front of nine people and two phones. By dinner, three of those phones have decided you are difficult to work with. You choose to refuse and demand a public mission. By The Doctor's Office, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Engage him cautiously to slow the deal
choices.consequence: You nod through forty minutes on mineral futures. He decides you're a friend, which is worse, because friends get texted at two in the morning.

nodes.text: By lunch you're a reaction GIF. By dinner you're a shirt. Somebody slows down the clip of you saying we are all going to die, drops a beat under it, and charts with it. Strangers tell you they love your energy. Your inbox holds nine hundred messages and not one is from an astronomer.

choices.text: Use the platform for science
choices.consequence: You post a careful thread with citations. It does four percent of the numbers the shirt did. You post it again anyway. You choose to use the platform for science. By The Doctor's Office, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Disappear from media and focus on the work
choices.consequence: You delete the apps and sleep eight hours for the first time in a month. The internet decides your silence proves you were lying. You commit to disappear from media and focus on the work. The road to The Whistle is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Your grad student is on something small and blue now, prescribed by a man who called the comet 'a lot to be holding.' Your best colleague resigns by email and drives to a cabin with no signal. The dean asks, over a fruit plate, whether your tone might be softened. For the department. For giving.

choices.text: Refuse to soften
choices.consequence: You tell the dean the tone is the data. He says he admires that, and moves your office to the building with the smell. You refuse to soften. It gets you to The Tour, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Soften enough to stay employed
choices.consequence: You start saying 'concerning' where you used to say 'fatal.' Nobody argues with you all week, which turns out to be its own punishment. You soften enough to stay employed. It gets you to The Senate Hearing, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: A padded envelope, no return address, postmarked Houston. Inside: 340 pages of internal scheduling and one highlighted line sliding the deflection launch eleven weeks right to accommodate 'partner payload integration.' The partner is Peter. Somebody at NASA has committed a felony to mail you a Gantt chart. You read it twice standing in the driveway.

choices.text: Leak it to the press
choices.consequence: You hand it to a reporter in a parking garage, because that is apparently how this is done. She asks if you have anything shorter. You commit to leak it to the press. The road to The Tour is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Take it to a senator who will hold a hearing
choices.consequence: You take the slow legal route, which buys you legitimacy, a subpoena, and roughly nine weeks you did not have to spend. You choose to take it to a senator who will hold a hearing. By The Senate Hearing, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Forty-one towns. Gymnasiums, VFW halls, one back room at an Applebee's with the projector propped on a phone book. The questions are better than anything you got in Washington: a kid in Ohio asks about ejecta velocity and gets the units right. You lose your voice in Tulsa and finish the week on a whiteboard.

choices.text: Keep touring until the deflection date
choices.consequence: You add nine more towns and start sleeping sitting up. Your daughter texts you photographs of dinners you weren't at, no caption. You keep touring until the deflection date. It gets you to The Movement, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Pause to rest with your family
choices.consequence: You cancel Nebraska and sleep fourteen hours. Somewhere in hour nine you stop dreaming in orbital mechanics, which feels like both a betrayal and a mercy.

nodes.text: Two networks carry it live; a third runs a banner about a missing yacht. You explain impact energy in joules, then, when pressed, in Hiroshimas, which is the number that finally lands in the room. The senator who called the hearing has a fundraising email out before you finish. Subject line: I DEMANDED ANSWERS.

choices.text: Confront the senator on her tactics
choices.consequence: You catch her in the hallway. She agrees with every word you say, warmly, then asks if you'd headline a donor breakfast in Sacramento. You confront the senator on her tactics. It gets you to The Movement, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Take the win — congressional record matters
choices.consequence: You let it go. Page 4,111 of the congressional record now contains the actual number, where somebody may find it in forty years. You choose to take the win — congressional record matters. By Your Family, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: They're in a park in the rain with laminated signs and one word on their shirts: LOOK. A retired machinist who watched Apollo on a black-and-white shows you a scale model he built in his garage, correct to the kilometer. Somebody's kid hands you a granola bar. For about nine minutes you think this is winnable.

choices.text: Join the movement as a public face
choices.consequence: You take the megaphone and it feeds back. Ten thousand people cheer a scientist who has never once enjoyed being looked at. You commit to join the movement as a public face. The road to The Deflection Mission Launches is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Support quietly from the lab
choices.consequence: You send them the real numbers, formatted for poster board, and stay home. The machinist puts your equations on a bedsheet and it beats any keynote.

nodes.text: Your daughter, twelve, asks if you want to go skating Saturday. Not in a meaningful way. In the way you'd ask someone to pass the salt. You do the arithmetic and find you have not been skating with her in two years. She says it's fine either way. She has learned to say that.

choices.text: Go skating
choices.consequence: You fall twice on public ice while a man films it for the internet. Your daughter laughs so hard she has to hold the wall. You go skating. It gets you to The Deflection Mission Launches, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Reschedule for after the deflection date
choices.consequence: You say after the launch, and she says sure, and writes it on the fridge calendar in pen, which is either faith or evidence. You reschedule for after the deflection date. It gets you to Peter's Plan Fails, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Eight rockets: five American, two European, one Japanese with a crane painted on the fairing. The desert viewing party has a taco truck and nobody is eating. When the stack clears the tower, a woman behind you says 'go' very quietly, over and over, the way you'd talk to a horse.

choices.text: Trust the math you signed off on
choices.consequence: You put the tablet face down and watch it with your eyes, like a person. The math will be the math whether or not you refresh. You commit to trust the math you signed off on. The road to Three Months Out is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Stay on alert for the abort signal
choices.consequence: You refresh telemetry every nine seconds for four hours. Every number is perfect. You do not once look up at the actual sky. You choose to stay on alert for the abort signal. By The Dinner Table, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: His rockets go up fourteen weeks late and come apart in a manner his own engineers described, in writing, twice. The comet does not deflect. It wobbles, politely. Peter blames the modeling, the media, and a former employee. The country, for one glorious afternoon, agrees on a single thing: this one is Peter's.

choices.text: Push for the backup public mission, faster
choices.consequence: You spend nineteen hours on the phone being right, which nobody enjoys, and by dawn the backup stack has a fueling window. You choose to push for the backup public mission, faster. By Three Months Out, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Begin preparing the public for impact in 60 days
choices.consequence: You start writing the sentence that tells three hundred million people what's coming. Draft nine is three hundred words shorter than draft one.

nodes.text: The deflection worked, mostly. Then a Chilean array finds a piece that snapped off in the shove: four hundred meters, still on intercept. Not a planet-killer. A city-killer, a phrase you now have to say into a microphone. Every equation gets redone live on television by four people arguing about one decimal.

choices.text: Push for evacuation of the projected zone
choices.consequence: You argue for moving two million people on the strength of a probability cone. Someone asks what happens if you're wrong. You say: traffic. You commit to push for evacuation of the projected zone. The road to The Evacuation is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Push for a second, smaller deflection
choices.consequence: You back the harder shot. One rocket, one window, eleven weeks to build it. The engineers stop sleeping and turn unbearable, which means it's working.

nodes.text: Three weeks out and the whole country eats at six, like a nation of farmers. Your family does the thing where everyone reaches for the bread at once. Your daughter holds your hand under the table. Somewhere inside this catastrophe you became a decent parent, which is a rude way to find out.

choices.text: Stay home for the last weeks
choices.consequence: You cancel everything and learn to make a passable risotto. It takes four attempts. Nobody in this house has anywhere else to be. You commit to stay home for the last weeks. The road to The Evacuation is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Go on the road for one last week of public service
choices.consequence: You do seven cities in six days, because somebody has to stand in a gym and answer the question honestly. Your family drives you to the airport.

nodes.text: They move two million people in nineteen days: buses, church vans, one man with a horse trailer doing seven round trips. It's ragged and slow and forty-one people flatly refuse. The fragment comes down three hundred kilometers offshore. The wave takes the boardwalk, the marina, two towns. Not the towns you emptied.

choices.text: Help with the long recovery
choices.consequence: You put your name on a clipboard rota and stay. The work is folding chairs and phone numbers, and nobody films any of it. You help with the long recovery. It gets you to FEMA Trailer Coffee, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

choices.text: Step back and write a book about the politics of it
choices.consequence: You take the advance and a small office with a window. Writing it down is the only way you will ever stop saying it out loud. You commit to step back and write a book about the politics of it. The road to The Chapter on Peter is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Whatever the sky is doing, you all sit down at 7:15. The wine is a supermarket red with a kangaroo on the label. Your brother-in-law tells the beach story where your father lost the cooler to a wave, and the details are wrong, and nobody corrects him, and you laugh until you have to set the glass down.

choices.text: Make this the meal
choices.consequence: You stop checking your phone at the table for the first time in nine months. The pie is store-bought. The pie is completely fine. You choose to make this the meal. By Tea, Three A.M., the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Make the morning a phone call to anyone you still owe one
choices.consequence: You start a list on a napkin. It reaches nineteen names before dessert, and four of them are people who once fired you. You choose to make the morning a phone call to anyone you still owe one. By Tea, Three A.M., the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: A parking lot, a clipboard, and coffee of clipboard grade. You walk a displaced family of six through form 4-B while their youngest sleeps on a duffel bag. You know the composition of a comet's nucleus. Today, the useful skill is knowing which box gets the trailer, and you had to be taught it Tuesday.

choices.text: Stay in the field for the long recovery
choices.consequence: You sign on for another eighteen months and learn the paperwork properly. Nobody in this lot has ever heard of you, which is restful. You commit to stay in the field for the long recovery. The road to After is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Move to the policy side after a year
choices.consequence: You take a policy job after a year and discover you can move a thousand trailers with one memo, and it feels like nothing at all. You move to the policy side after a year. It gets you to The Book, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Eleven at night, office lamp, the chapter on Peter. It comes out in one go and it is meaner than the rest of the book by a full register. You reread it and understand it was never for the reader. The cursor sits there. It's a hundred and four pages either way; the only question is where.

choices.text: Lead with it; name the cost
choices.consequence: You put it in chapter two and name every number he ignored. Two publishers get nervous. The lawyers bill for a week and cut one adjective. You choose to lead with it; name the cost. By The Book, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Bury it; let the science breathe first
choices.consequence: You move it to an appendix so the science gets the front of the book. It is the more honest choice and it tastes like sand. You choose to bury it; let the science breathe first. By After, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The house ticks. You boil water you don't want and stand there while the kettle works itself up. Across the way the neighbor's kitchen is lit too, and neither of you is going to mention this tomorrow. Two mugs are out on the counter. You don't remember getting the second one down. Everyone in Tea, Three A.M.

choices.text: Make breakfast for whoever wakes first
choices.consequence: You get out the good pan and six eggs. It's the least scientific decision you've made in thirty years and by far the easiest. You commit to make breakfast for whoever wakes first. The road to Dinner, Together is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

choices.text: Start the list of calls before sunrise
choices.consequence: You start dialing at 5:40 a.m., which is a violent hour to be forgiven in. Three people pick up on the first ring. You choose to start the list of calls before sunrise. By The Phone Calls, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: You spend a decade on preparedness: hearings, budget lines, a standing committee with terrible coffee. You become a man who returns calls from staffers named Braden. Nobody makes a shirt of you. A woman in Ohio names her telescope after you and you find out three years later from a form letter. The next crop of graduate students finds you boring, which is precisely the point. You are tired. You are useful. It'll do.

The book is assigned in three graduate programs and misquoted in thirty. The chapter on Peter is the one people underline. When the next rock comes — smaller, closer, handled in nine weeks flat — a deputy administrator cites page 212 on live television and mispronounces your name. You sign copies for students born after the night you stood on a soundstage and said the number out loud. You have never been happier to be a footnote.

The world does whatever the world does. What's true is this: you ate together, the potatoes were oversalted, and your daughter told a joke with a long setup and no punchline and everyone laughed at the wrong part. You held hands. You said the honest thing quietly, once, and then let it be. Nobody does the dishes. It's allowed. The credits, if there are any, roll on a kitchen with the light still on.

By sunrise you've called nineteen people: two exes, your thesis adviser, the man whose grant you torpedoed in 2009. Four apologies, twelve thank-yous, three voicemails that ramble badly. The adviser cries. The 2009 man says he'd have done the same thing, then asks after your daughter by name. Whatever comes next, you go into it as roughly the person you meant to be. Give or take. Mostly take.
